item.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude (154 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/designing-efficient-quantum-circuits, See on Hacker News

Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.

This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv.

Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition—which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.

The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.

Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.

In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)

Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.1

These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits. These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.

We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2). 

In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.

Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.

These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.

A new reversible algorithm

Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs. 

The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.

This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.

This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.

A hard first test: modular inversion

The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself n times, find n. For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.

These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.

We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.

The memory demands of divsteps

Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called modular inversion. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer a, find x such that ax ≡ 1 (mod p). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called divsteps. Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.

Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called branch information, is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.

How Claude got around the memory problem

Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.

To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.

Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.

A family of designs

Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).

Optimizing a quantum optimizer

Optimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is one of the strongest candidates for offering a superpolynomial quantum speedup—an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.

When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.

A more efficient quantum decoder

The researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position x contains several acceptable values of y. The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many x positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed–Solomon decoder.

Reed–Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a syndrome. The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.

Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at Google Quantum AI imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on Frontier, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed–Solomon decoding.

So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp–Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp–Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.

A simplified approach to storage

Switching to Berlekamp–Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information.

Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.

Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).

Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp–Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.

What we learned

Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.

Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.

Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones. 

We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.

Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost. 

This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.

item.title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks (540 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/, See on Hacker News

The Benchmark Map

Each tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks.

All 22 job families

click a family to open it

Coverage by

Covered with at least

  • Benchmark Index
  • No coverage

In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts, and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.

Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.

The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:

For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.

As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.

Methodology in brief

To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.

To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:

  • Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.
  • Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.
  • Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.
  • Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.
  • Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.

Following work by Wang et al., we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.

To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al.’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.

A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.

Limitations

Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.

We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).

By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.

Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

Patterns in coverage

The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al.), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.

But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:

After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:

The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.

Can O*NET + benchmarks tell us how good AI is at your job?

Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.

We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.

O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average, we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.

As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar:

In this case, at least, O*NET weighting changes very little. Model performance on APEX prompts is similar across the O*NET tasks included in the weighted scores above, which limits the value of reweighting. However, less than ⅓ of the O*NET tasks relevant to the 4 occupations above have enough APEX coverage to be included in our weighted scores. We are hopeful that applying O*NET weighting to a much larger set of benchmarks will result in high-quality occupation-specific model scores, and are working toward that goal.

However, even if we incorporate tasks from dozens of benchmarks, several obstacles remain:

  1. 01

    How do we navigate low statistical power?

    The sheer breadth of work done in the US economy means that for any O*NET occupation and task, we have relatively few benchmark items. This means that our estimates are inherently underpowered, and just one or two low-quality items can severely bias our scores.

  2. 02

    How do we account for the varying difficulty and fidelity of tasks?

    Some benchmark items are highly saturated, whereas others are still unsolved. This is partly a function of time (as older benchmarks were designed for less performant models and simpler environments) and partly a function of quality (some benchmark items are simplistically graded, have minor mistakes, or can be reward hacked). We do not yet have an explicit way of weighting by quality.

  3. 03

    Can evals that primarily measure AI automation generalize to augmentation?

    In the real world, AI models are still primarily used by humans, rather than automating entire job functions end-to-end. Therefore, measuring the real-world occupation capabilities of a model should ideally include measuring how much the model augments human productivity. We have completed some early work in this direction, but finding a methodology that scales remains elusive.

  4. 04

    Can every O*NET occupation and task be measured with benchmarks?

    Knowledge-based work is well-suited to measurement through benchmarks because it is largely done on digital machines, like laptops and phones. Dingel and Neiman estimate that only 37% of US jobs could feasibly be done entirely from home, suggesting that ~63% of jobs involve some tasks with a physical-world component which would be hard to incorporate into current benchmarks. For now, this may not be a meaningful oversight – with the rapid development of robotics capabilities, we anticipate a significant need for physical task benchmarks.

We are actively working on these problems; if you are too, please reach out!

We are indebted to Wang et al. for the O*NET tagging methodology, and thank Nathan Lambert for feedback on a draft of this work.

item.title: Desire to Move Permanently to U.S. at New Low (196 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://news.gallup.com/poll/708614/desire-migrate-drops-new-low.aspx, See on Hacker News

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. remains the most desired destination for people who would like to leave their own countries permanently, but Gallup's latest data show it is less attractive than it once was.

In 2025, 15% of adults worldwide who say they would like to move permanently to another country name the U.S. as their preferred destination, the lowest level recorded in nearly two decades of Gallup research. From 2007 to 2009, 24% of would-be migrants named the U.S. as their top choice, and that figure remained near 20% through 2016. Since 2017, it has been at or below 18%.

The rank order of the countries attracting the most interest from potential migrants has seen little change since Gallup’s first measure. Canada ranks second, as it has for several years, with 9% of potential migrants mentioning the U.S. neighbor. The appeal of these desired destinations did not change in 2025, even as the U.S. became less desirable.

Line charts show trends in the percentage of adults worldwide who would like to move permanently to top destination countries from 2007–2009 to 2025. The United States remains the top destination but declines from 24% to 15%. Canada rises from 7% to 9%. The United Kingdom declines from 7% to 4%. Germany, Australia, Spain, France, Japan, Italy, and Saudi Arabia remain broadly stable around 3% to 5%.

Gallup's latest update on migration desire is based on a question asked almost annually: “Ideally, if you had the opportunity, would you like to move permanently to another country, or would you prefer to continue living in this country?” Those who say they would like to move are then asked to name their preferred destination.

Results for 2025 are based on interviews with over 144,000 adults in 140 countries. The current estimates include data from China for 2023, the last time the question was asked there.

The most recent analysis period coincides with a sharp slowdown in international migration into the U.S., amid changes in immigration policy and declining migration desire in several regions. External data suggest global migration more broadly slowed in 2024 after surging post-pandemic.

Declining Desire to Move to the U.S.

The U.S. became less attractive to adults in several regions in 2025, with statistically significant declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia.

Latin America accounts for seven of the 16 countries worldwide where the percentage naming the U.S. as a preferred destination fell by at least 10 points. In the region, the percentage fell from 33% in 2024 to 28% in 2025.

Other Latin American countries that saw double-digit declines include U.S. neighbor Mexico, where the latest 21% who want to move to the U.S. matches the previous low set in 2017 and 2018. In Honduras, desire to migrate to the U.S. dropped 35 percentage points, from 71% to 36%, the largest decline in any country in 2025.

###Embeddable###

Despite the falling numbers, the U.S. remains by far the most desired destination in Latin America and the Caribbean and in sub-Saharan Africa. The picture varies more in other regions.

In Southeast Asia, Japan leads at 23%, compared with 12% for the U.S. In the Middle East and North Africa, Germany attracts 13% and Saudi Arabia 12% of potential migrants, with the U.S. at 9%. In South Asia, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. are roughly tied, each cited by 7%. Within the European Union, Spain, at 11%, and Switzerland, at 8%, rank ahead of the U.S., at 6%.

Global Desire to Migrate Falls, Shifts

Beyond where people want to go, the data also show a shift in how many want to move at all.

Overall, global desire to migrate declined in 2025 to its lowest level in a decade, driven by sharp drops in regions that have long had the highest migration aspirations, including Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. After holding at a record-high 16% between 2021 and 2024, global desire dipped in 2025 for the first time in years, falling one point to 15%, a level not seen since 2018.

###Embeddable###

In Latin America and the Caribbean, 25% of adults say they would like to move permanently to another country, the lowest level in a decade. The decline is particularly notable in this region, where migration desire has fallen steadily after peaking at 34% in 2021-2022.

Multiple countries across the region recorded double-digit declines between 2024 and 2025. In Honduras and El Salvador, the percentage of adults wanting to leave fell sharply last year, from levels above 50% in several prior years to 35% and 25%, respectively.

In sub-Saharan Africa, where migration desire remains the highest globally, 33% say they would like to move permanently, also a decade low. As recently as 2023, that figure stood at 37%, ticking upward from 36% in 2021-2022.

In regions that are typically on the receiving end of migrants, the picture is different. Migration desire in the United States and Canada (20%) and the European Union (21%) remains near record highs.

In the U.S., notably, the heightened desire to move abroad is concentrated among women younger than 45. In 2025, 40% of U.S. women aged 15 to 44 say they would move permanently to another country if they had the opportunity, up from 10% in 2014. The trend first rose sharply in 2016 and continued across multiple years, suggesting a broader shift in outlook rather than a short-term political effect.

Bottom Line

It is important to note that desire to migrate is not the same as intent to move. Not everyone who wants to move can or will do so. The 2025 data show that fewer people worldwide are imagining their futures elsewhere, and the U.S., long the world’s most desired destination, is attracting less of that interest than at any point in nearly two decades.

For years, the dominant story in global migration data was a rising desire to move across nearly every region. The 2025 data suggest that pattern is shifting. The declines are widespread and concentrated in the regions that have historically driven global migration.

At the same time, the picture is not uniform. In regions that typically receive migrants, including the U.S. and Canada, along with the EU, desire to leave remains near record highs. And within the U.S., a growing number of younger women say they would move abroad permanently if they could.

These patterns show that interest in moving abroad, and to the U.S. in particular, is shifting across regions. But despite these changes, many people worldwide — an estimated 900 million — would like to move, including about 134 million who would prefer to move to the U.S.

Read Gallup’s analysis of how these shifts in migration desire could translate into changes in population size and human capital across countries.

Andrew Dugan and Michelle Chau contributed to this analysis.

item.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases (285 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jakearchibald.com/2026/jpeg-xl-vs-avif/, See on Hacker News

JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.

Conclusions

I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:

For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.

The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel, a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl, except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.

For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.

For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data.

AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.

AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.

Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.

AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.

Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data.

Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data.

AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself.

For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples.

JPEG XL can make existing JPEGs 9–20% smaller, without further loss. It's also as fast or faster to decode, except for small images. See the data.

For lossless, JPEG XL is the clear winner. Lossless WebP is 9–17% larger for photos, and lossless AVIF is 30–120% larger. But lossless images are almost never what you want on the web. If you do use them on the web (like I do on this page), watch out for jixel's higher efforts - it often produces files that are too slow to decode. See the data.

Animated image formats continue to be a dumb idea. Please don't use them. Learn more, if you must.

For web use-cases, I'd currently default to AVIF 4:4:4, with the highest effort level I can be bothered with. If I felt AVIF was producing an unusually large file, I'd take a look at JPEG XL via jixel, and see if it did better.

Both AVIF and JPEG XL (via jixel) have seen massive improvements recently, so it's possible that this recommendation could change in future. There's been a lot of misinformation around this stuff, and your AI will happily deliver that misinformation to you. Instead, test things with your own images.

AVIF folks suggest that JPEG XL is technically limited compared to AVIF. That might be true, but in this article I'm focusing on results with today's implementations.

Methodology

I 'created' a benchmarking script, that encodes images using various codecs at various settings, and records various details.

I'm using the latest released versions of the image codecs, which at time of writing is:

  • avifenc 1.4.2
  • libjxl 0.12.0 (using its cjxl encoder)
  • jixel 0.4.2 (git f487299), a second JPEG XL encoder
  • cwebp 1.6.0 (lossless WebP is used later in the article)

I chose a selection of images, and encoded most of them to a width of 1598 pixels - which is 2x the maximum width images appear on this blog. This means they look sharp on high density displays, which most users have. As a result, if you're viewing this on a small or low density screen, you're not getting the full experience.

I ran these benchmarks on my 2024 MacBook Pro (M4 Pro).

Lossy - F1 image

When I first wrote about AVIF, I used an F1 car as the first image, so I figured I'd do that again!

I encoded the image at various codec qualities, and chose versions that were closest to particular SSIMULACRA2 scores - a perceptual image quality metric by the folks behind JPEG XL. 50 is considered medium quality, 70 high, 80 very high, and 90 visually lossless. Although, I'm not sure if these ratings take high density displays into account.

Throughout the article, the visual comparisons, like above, use each encoder's maximum effort, except in cases where maximum effort results in a larger file (yes, that happens).

For archival, I'd tend towards near-lossless qualities, but if I'm just displaying an illustrative image on my blog, performance is more important to me. I'm personally happy with the 70 result above. If you zoom in, you can see the quality loss, but if I was really concerned about the zoom-in case, I'd use something like the VisualViewport API to load in a higher resolution image when that happens, rather than make the download bigger for everyone.

At lower qualities you can see the difference in strategy between the codecs. The detail loss is around the same, but AVIF tends to smooth things out compared to the original, whereas JPEG XL seems to introduce rougher patterns.

Progressive

Both AVIF and JPEG XL are capable of showing something progressively as the image loads. Chrome and Firefox support progressive JPEG XL, whereas only Chrome supports progressive AVIF. So, and I say this through gritted teeth, this next demo is best viewed in Chrome (I have a Firefox patch in progress):

This is the 18 megapixel image again, so if you're viewing this on a device with a smaller screen, you're not getting the full effect.

Progressive AVIF and JPEG XL work very differently. With JPEG XL, you can opt into the data being stored in such a way that a decoder can render low resolution versions, before it brings in the higher resolution tiles. jixel recently (like, yesterday at time of writing) added support for this too. It's called "progressive DC", and it's the most important kind of progressive rendering for JPEG XL.

With AVIF, progressions work more like frames of a video. You provide up to four frames, so that's three phases before the final image. Again, like a video, each frame can use data from the previous frame as an optimisation. An advantage of this is you can choose exactly how those frames look. In the example above, I went with a single preview frame: a 1/8th resolution version, with a bit of blurring. But, your preview frames can be completely different images if you really want.

There's a lack of data when it comes to progressive images and user experience, so these are just my reckons:

If you're on a bad connection, data doesn't arrive gradually like some throttling tools will have you believe. It tends to come in bursts. So, there's little benefit to progressive rendering on smaller images, and I'm not sure that many progressive phases is particularly useful.

I think that it's nice to have a representative preview for images that may take some time to load. I've experienced this personally, where a site or app has given me something clearly not-loaded, but with enough detail to know what's coming. That's useful to me, as I can decide things like, if it's worth waiting for the whole thing. This is also why I think things like BlurHash are cute, but useless. They're not a representative preview, so there's little a user can do with the information provided.

The preview frame I chose for the AVIF is enough to tell it's an open-wheel race car. If you know F1, you'll know what team it is. You might even know where the photo was taken. And it delivers that in ~11.5 kB.

The JPEG XL gets a BlurHash-like preview on screen in ~2 kB, but it takes until ~63 kB to match the preview quality of the AVIF. After that, it continues to improve gradually, providing a more detailed and higher quality image as more data arrives.

However, I'm not convinced this is a good user experience, as it presents the user with something they may mistake for fully-loaded, but poor quality. For example:

Here's a crop of the JPEG XL, 80% loaded. It seems reasonable that someone would look at that, and just assume I took the picture badly, leaving parts out of focus. You could probably convince me that blurring the ApeCoin logo is a societal benefit, but it still feels like a suboptimal user experience.

AVIF's system gives me more control, but it's also more complex.

Progressive overhead

I encoded the large F1 image with and without progressive rendering enabled, adjusting the quality setting to keep the SSIMULACRA2 score around 70:

  • With libjxl, progressive is basically free. In fact, it produced files 6–10% smaller. At default effort, it was also faster to encode, and used less memory. Decoding was ~10% faster in Firefox, but 12–20% slower in Chrome and Safari.
  • With jixel, it depends on the effort. For jixel, I used progressive DC, with the centre of the image loading first. At jixel's default ('fast'), progressive made the file 12% bigger. At 'extraslow', it made the file 10% smaller, and 11% faster to encode, although it used 17% more memory. Decoding was barely affected, other than being 7–9% slower in Chrome.
  • But ColorVideoVDP is less kind to progressive jixel. It rates jixel's progressive files slightly lower than the non-progressive versions, whereas it rates libjxl's progressive files slightly higher. Taking that into account, progressive jixel at 'extraslow' is only ~2% smaller than non-progressive, and at 'fast' it's around 18% bigger.
  • Regular progressive AVIF has a bigger cost when it comes to encoding. It uses around twice the memory, and at default effort (s6), it takes twice as long to encode. At s0, encode time is only 9% longer, but the file is 14% bigger. And this is pure encode time - it doesn't factor in how you might generate the preview frame, e.g. adding some blur.
  • Regular progressive AVIF is 29–44% slower to decode in Chrome, although the difference is smaller in other browsers (6–15%). Since Chrome is the only browser that supports rendering the progressive frames, that might explain it. Although Firefox and Safari are still having to decode the progressive frame, as the main image builds upon it.
  • With AVIF, making the final frame a keyframe fixes the decoding overhead, at the cost of a longer encode time. At maximum effort, it results in a smaller file too, only 3–5% bigger than the non-progressive version. You could call this cheating, as there's now no 'progression' in terms of data - it's just two images in one. But, if it's a better user experience, who cares?
  • Even with the overhead, progressive AVIF wins on decoding time, and usually on file size. The progressive AVIFs are 152–181 kB. jixel's 'extraslow' progressive JPEG XL is in that range at 166 kB, but jixel's default produces 252 kB, and libjxl's progressive files are 233–242 kB. The AVIFs decode 1.6–6x faster, with the biggest gap in Safari, which is particularly slow to decode jixel's files.

Lossy - HDR

Let's get back to lossy compression, but this time HDR! There are a few ways to encode HDR images, and we're going to look at two.

Perceptual Quantization (PQ) tells each pixel what to be. Each value maps to an absolute brightness, up to 10,000 nits, with the curve shaped so the data is spent where our eyes are most sensitive. If the image asks for colours and brightnesses the display can't show (no consumer display can hit 10,000 nits), the browser/OS has to tone-map it down, and how well that's done varies between platforms.

Gain maps are different. The main image is a regular SDR image (usually), and alongside it is a 'gain map', which applies a brightness and colour change to each pixel to achieve the HDR version.

This has two benefits:

  1. The same image will look exactly as you want on an SDR display - the gain map is simply ignored.
  2. If the display supports HDR, but maybe not as much as the image needs (for example, the screen is at low or maximum brightness), the browser/OS can apply as much of the gain map as it can handle.

CSS and <picture> let us serve an SDR or PQ image to the user via the dynamic-range media query, but then you're relying on tone mapping in cases where the browser signals HDR support, but it doesn't support the full range.

Although the JPEG XL format supports gain maps, no browser handles them, and the encoding story is messy.

AVIF supports gain maps, and you encode them by providing two images: the SDR image and the HDR image. It uses those to calculate and encode the gain map.

Your browser/screen doesn't support HDR, so the PQ images will look bad.

At medium brightnesses, on an HDR screen, the gain map and PQ images look the same. At maximum brightnesses, on my Pixel 10 Pro and 2024 MacBook Pro, the PQ images get a bit blown out, and the gain map image looks better. At low brightness on my Pixel 10 Pro, again the gain map image looks better.

This is because, at extreme brightness levels, the device doesn't have the full HDR headroom to display the image, and gain maps can handle these cases better. So, although gain maps seem to add a lot to the file size, I think it's worth it.

Maybe there's a future where tone mapping gets much better, and the advantage of a gain map becomes less significant.

Regular SSIMULACRA2 only understands SDR, so for this image, the scores come from an experimental HDR mode in fast-ssim2. That means these scores can't be compared to the SSIMULACRA2 scores elsewhere in this article. ColorVideoVDP handles HDR natively, and here it's modelling a 1,500 nit HDR monitor.

The two metrics disagree a lot with this image. And they don't factor in the benefits of gain maps, so treat these results as a comparison between the PQ variants:

  • File size: JPEG XL wins, but the metrics disagree on how much, and with which encoder.
    • According to HDR SSIMULACRA2, jixel's default ranges from 8% smaller to 3% larger than PQ AVIF's default, and libjxl is 5–33% larger. At maximum efforts, jixel 'extraslow' is up to 15% smaller than PQ AVIF s0.
    • According to ColorVideoVDP, libjxl is the clear winner. At default efforts, it's 28–53% smaller than PQ AVIF, and 17–37% smaller than gain map AVIF. At maximum efforts, it's up to 23% smaller than the best AVIF, but jixel 'extraslow' is roughly level with it, ranging from 12% smaller to 14% larger.
  • The metrics also disagree about gain maps. HDR SSIMULACRA2 says gain map AVIF is 31–38% larger than PQ AVIF, but ColorVideoVDP says gain map AVIF is 11–25% smaller than PQ AVIF.
  • Encode time: JPEG XL (jixel) wins. At default efforts, jixel is ~2x faster than PQ AVIF, and produces files around the same size or smaller, depending on the metric. libjxl's default is 5–47% slower than PQ AVIF, but given ColorVideoVDP's view of the file sizes, that's a reasonable trade. Gain map AVIF is the slowest, as it's calculating a gain map, then essentially encoding two images: ~3x slower than PQ AVIF.
  • Encode memory: JPEG XL (jixel) wins. At default efforts, jixel uses ~30% less memory than PQ AVIF. libjxl's default uses ~1.9x the memory of PQ AVIF, and gain map AVIF uses ~1.55x. At maximum efforts, libjxl uses ~6x the memory of PQ AVIF's default, and jixel 'extraslow' uses ~10x.
  • Decode time: AVIF wins. PQ and gain map AVIF decode at around the same speed. JPEG XL takes 1.2–1.7x as long to decode in Chrome, although it's slightly faster at the top of the quality range. In Safari, it takes 1.6–3x as long. Firefox is particularly slow with these HDR JPEG XL images, taking ~4x as long as AVIF at all qualities. We're working on it.
  • Higher effort is worth it for AVIF. For gain map AVIF, s5 gets you 9–12% smaller files for ~1.9x the encode time, and s0 gets you 14–20% smaller files for ~11x the encode time. For PQ AVIF, s0 gets you 14–19% smaller files, for 17–20x the encode time.
  • Higher effort is worth it for jixel, up to 'slow'. 'slow' gets you 7–32% smaller files than its default 'fast', for ~3.8x the encode time. 'extraslow' saves another 1–9%, but takes ~10x longer than 'slow' and uses ~8.5x the memory. jixel only has a few data points for this image, so these numbers are rough.
  • Higher effort isn't worth it for libjxl. libjxl's maximum effort gets you 2–7% smaller files than its default, but takes ~15x longer.

It will be interesting to see how JPEG XL handles gain maps once they're fully supported.

By the way, these are signs that indicate whether my cats are inside or outside, and the little display indicates how long until their next automated feed.

JPEG transcoding

JPEG XL allows you to convert an existing JPEG to JPEG XL without additional loss. I tested this with the F1 image at a range of sizes and JPEG qualities:

  • The JPEG XL is 9–20% smaller than the JPEG. The saving grows with resolution, from ~9% at 400 pixels wide to ~20% at 4,900 pixels wide. The saving is slightly smaller at higher JPEG qualities. libjxl and jixel produce practically identical file sizes.
  • For small images, JPEG XL is slower to decode than JPEG, taking 1.4–2.7x as long, depending on the browser. But it's just a millisecond or two.
  • For larger images, JPEG XL is faster to decode in Chrome and Safari. From ~1,000 pixels wide, it matches JPEG, and at the largest sizes, it decodes in around half the time. In Firefox, it ends up around the same speed as JPEG.
  • jixel's output is slightly slower to decode than libjxl's in Chrome and Firefox, by up to ~25%. But again, these are small numbers, at most a few milliseconds.

Of course, if you have the original, you'd be way better off creating a proper new lossy version with AVIF or JPEG XL, but it's pretty cool that the JPEGs end up smaller, and sometimes faster to decode. Although, I suppose this is just pointing to a missing optimisation in browser JPEG decoders.

Show me the graphs!

Lossless

It is very rare to need lossless images on the web. As we've already seen, even for things like screenshots and illustrations, lossy AVIF handles them really well. Ironically, this page is one of the outliers, because I wanted to show the compressed versions vs their lossless counterparts. Thankfully, JPEG XL is great at lossless!

The results:

  • File size: JPEG XL wins. At default efforts, libjxl produces the smallest files for every image except the illustration, where WebP matches it. WebP is 9–17% larger for photos, and AVIF is 33–122% larger. At highest efforts, libjxl and jixel are within a few percent of each other, WebP is 5–44% larger, and AVIF is 29–176% larger.
  • Encode time: JPEG XL wins. libjxl's default takes 0.1–0.5 seconds, which is faster than WebP's default, and similar to AVIF's default, while producing smaller files than both.
  • Encode memory: JPEG XL wins or WebP wins, depending on the image. WebP's default uses around half the memory of libjxl's default (55–110 MB vs 110–250 MB), but libjxl's files are smaller. For photos, WebP can't match libjxl's default file size even at its maximum effort, which uses more memory than libjxl's default. For the screenshot, they use around the same memory, but libjxl's file is smaller. The illustration is the exception: WebP's maximum effort produces a file 20% smaller than libjxl's default, using the same memory.
  • Decode time: WebP wins or JPEG XL wins, depending on the image. WebP decodes photos in 17–39 ms in all browsers, and the screenshot in ~5 ms. libjxl's output takes 1–2.2x as long in Chrome, 1.4–2.7x as long in Firefox, and 2.1–3.2x as long in Safari. But for photos, JPEG XL's smaller files more than make up for this on a first load, unless the connection is really fast. For the screenshot and illustration, WebP's decode advantage wins. Lossless AVIF is particularly slow to decode, taking up to 4x as long as libjxl's output in Chrome.
  • Lossless AVIF is bad. It's significantly larger than the others, and slower to decode.
  • jixel's 'medium' setting is the sweet spot for file size. It beats libjxl's default on every image (0.5–23% smaller), and is within 2–3% of the best result for photos, taking 0.4–0.7 seconds. But it uses 470–670 MB of memory, and its output is slower to decode than libjxl's, particularly in Safari.
  • jixel's 'slow' and 'extraslow' output is very slow to decode for photos. ~200–290 ms, compared to 22–95 ms for libjxl's output. That's 2–13x slower, depending on the browser. It's also slow for the alpha image, at 80–123 ms compared to 14–27 ms for libjxl's output. This doesn't happen with the screenshot and illustration. This means, for my use-case on this page, I'd avoid it.
  • libjxl's maximum effort is very slow. It produces files 2–7% smaller than its default for photos, and ~25% smaller for the screenshot and illustration, but takes 9–46 seconds, which is 50–180x as long as its default. jixel gets the same results in a couple of seconds.
  • jixel's default 'fast' setting isn't great for lossless. It's the fastest encoder by far (40–80 ms), but its files are 16–32% larger than libjxl's default for photos, and ~80% larger for the screenshot and illustration.
  • jixel's patches feature helps a bit with the screenshot (4–9% smaller), but makes no difference to the illustration.

Animation

Animated image formats are dumb and animated JPEG XL is no exception. Video formats are better at video. They're built for it. They're optimised for it. Not just in terms of encoding, but also in terms of playback.

I encoded a short clip, and the animated AVIF was 725 kB, and the JPEG XL was 2.17 MB for the same ColorVideoVDP score (9.5).

The JPEG XL is super noisy compared to the AVIF, because each frame is encoded individually, and arttifacts land in different places per frame.

AVIF is basically the keyframe format of AV1 video, with a bunch of still-image-specific optimisations thrown in. Animated AVIF however, is pretty much just a repackaging of AV1 video. You can convert an AV1 MP4 to AVIF and back losslessly - it's just a container change. That's why it performs so much better, because it's built for motion.

However, animated AVIF plays like shit in Chrome and Safari. It's fine in Firefox, so this is purely an implementation problem. But… <video muted autoplay> is right there.

The interesting detail of animated AVIF is that it supports transparency, whereas AV1 video doesn't. But really, that just highlights that it's dumb that AV1 didn't support transparency.

No, I'm not adding a demo. I don't want it on my server. Use video formats for video.

And that's it!

I already gave you my conclusions at the start, so I guess I'm ready to hit publish.

I'm a little nervous about this, because discourse around JPEG XL can get a little… weird. I see a lot of conspiracy theories about Google trying to 'silence' JPEG XL, even though one of the leads of the project worked at Google, as part of a team that were working on JPEG XL. That same leader claimed that the post-COVID layoffs wouldn't have happened if companies simply used JPEG XL. I was recently called a racist for asking about JPEG XL use-cases. This kind of thing just doesn't happen with other technologies and standards I follow. So, urm, I'm kinda bracing for impact here.

My first version of this article was very negative about JPEG XL, but then I heard about jixel, and honestly, I'm really excited about it. There's serious competition between AVIF and JPEG XL now, and whoever wins, we'll all benefit from better image compression.

item.title: US Rep Announces Congressional Legislation to Protect Video Game Ownership (208 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ritchietorres.house.gov/posts/rep-torres-announces-power-to-the-players-act-legislation-to-ensure-gamers-own-their-games, See on Hacker News

Today, Rep. Ritchie Torres (NY-15) announced he will introduce the Power To The Players Act, legislation that would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations protecting consumers’ ability to own and play the video games they purchase.

Over the past few years, video game companies have moved toward digital-only games and consoles, removing the option to buy or use physical games. These digital games are often sold as revocable licenses rather than owned outright, leaving players dependent on the company’s continued support. NBA 2K25 is a clear example. The game, which retailed for $69.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the All-Star Edition, will be delisted from digital storefronts on October 30 and will have its online servers shut down on December 31, only two years after its initial release. No consumer should have a game they paid for pulled out from under them on a company’s arbitrary timeline.

“When you pay for a game, you should own it,” said Rep. Torres. “Consumers must have the right to own, the right to play, and the right to transfer the games they buy. A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale. Families in the Bronx and across the country save up to buy these games, and they deserve better than a license that can vanish at any time. The Power To The Players Act ensures consumers own what they buy and can keep playing long after a company moves on.”

Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it. Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down. 

The legislation aims to close the gap between buying a game and owning it. By preserving consumers’ ability to own and resell their games, the bill would ensure that players can keep playing the games they paid for with friends and family for years to come.

item.title: Postgres 19 delayed after AI reviewers find more bugs than humans can fix (200 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theregister.com/databases/2026/10/16/postgres-19-delayed-after-ai-reviewers-find-more-bugs-than-humans-can-fix/5303471, See on Hacker News

databases

Core devs revert up to 10 features, push release to November, and blame better tooling rather than vibe coding

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest iteration of the popular open source database, and held back an unusual number of features.

Once slated for release in late September or early October, PostgreSQL 19 is now expected to be generally available around November 19. Developers have also dropped between eight and 10 significant features.

Explaining the number of reverts — features whose rollouts have now been postponed to next year's release, PostgreSQL 20 — Peter Eisentraut, veep at EDB, a PostgreSQL support and consultancy, said the reason could be at least in part attributed to the LLM code reviews used by developers.

In a blog post, Eisentraut, who is a leading PostgreSQL committer, said some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix "quickly and during beta."

However, the introduction of LLM-assisted code review also uncovered a long tail of “relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases” which, in past times, developers might not have noticed until much later, most likely issuing bug fixes in the five years following launch. “With LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring at a list of forty defect reports. Even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time.”

When the big updates for PostgreSQL 19 were written, LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, we're told, but in the months leading up to the launch, the AI-supported reviews became better understood and more effective.

“The effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future development cycles,” Eisentraut said.

He was also at pains to point out that the reverts were not down to “vibe coding” in development, as the technique was not available when most of the new features were written.

Postgres was first proposed by Michael Stonebraker in 1986. In 1994, Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen replaced the query language POSTQUEL with SQL, and in 1995 made the database freely available and modifiable under a more permissive license, renaming it PostgreSQL. It has since become the most popular database among professional developers owing to the services the big three hyperscalers built on it as well as the range of wire-compatible distributed systems available.

Among the features pulled from the PostgreSQL 19 iteration is support for SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), which became part of the SQL standard in 2023. The feature provides syntax for exploring relationships between nodes connected by edges. PostgreSQL's implementation was removed over unresolved issues.

At the time, PostgreSQL contributor Tom Lane warned: "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20."

Despite the delay, Eisentraut promises PostgreSQL 19 will still be “a great release,” that includes REPACK CONCURRENTLY, which avoids the table-lock VACUUM FULL operation used to reclaim disk space.

“And it will be very robust, after all the additional scrutiny,” he said.

The features reverted from PostgreSQL 19 will likely make it into PostgreSQL 20. Just a few months ago, developers expected PostgreSQL 20 to have no new features, just bug fixes. Now, it is likely to have the new features left over from the earlier release, Eisentraut said.®

Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.

In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.
