« En tant qu’entreprise canadienne, nous sommes fiers d’élargir notre partenariat avec Waymo afin de contribuer à l’arrivée des services de transport de personnes à la demande par véhicules autonomes à Toronto, a déclaré Laura Dottori-Attanasio, présidente et cheffe de la direction d’Element Fleet Management. Ensemble, Element et Waymo contribueront à créer des possibilités d’emploi en mettant à profit l’expertise d’Element en gestion de flottes, ses capacités opérationnelles et ses solutions de mobilité intelligente pour soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle de flottes de véhicules autonomes, tout en assurant la fiabilité de leurs opérations. »

Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps, pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert. Cela représente 20 fois moins d’accidents de ce type.

La sécurité et l’accessibilité sont à la base de la mission de Waymo : devenir le service de conduite autonome auquel le public fait le plus confiance au monde. Nous sommes fiers de collaborer avec des organismes de premier plan qui œuvrent en faveur de l’accessibilité et de la mobilité, notamment BALANCE for Blind Adults, l’Institut national canadien pour les aveugles (INCA), Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians et Epilepsy Ontario.

« L’innovation qui favorise l’autonomie est au cœur de tout ce que nous faisons. L’expérience de Waymo en matière de collaboration avec des personnes ayant une déficience visuelle pour concevoir des solutions accessibles est encourageante. Sa décision de nous consulter dès le début montre qu’une telle approche peut donner des résultats concrets », a déclaré Michelle McQuigge, PDG de BALANCE for Blind Adults.

Nous sommes ravis d’aider les résidents et les visiteurs à découvrir tout ce que Toronto a à offrir. Si vous avez envie de faire l’essai du Waymo Driver à Toronto, inscrivez-vous pour recevoir nos mises à jour et être parmi les premiers informés du lancement de notre service : waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.

item.title: Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD (188 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://calif.io/research/big-fish, See on Hacker News

Big fish. Small counter. Root shell.

Calif frequently publishes our offensive research and work, but we otherwise don't draw much attention to the defensive work we do — assisting open source projects with remediation, patch generation, cryptographic improvements, and internal engineering projects we carry out for our clients.

Earlier this year, we reported some vulnerabilities, often along with suggested patches to OpenBSD. One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources, where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value. This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root. The issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018, respectively.

The exploit

We managed to get local root in OpenBSD with KARL / SMAP / SMEP enabled without the use of an information disclosure vulnerability via the following path:

  • Map 127 SysV shared memory segments, unmap them via munmap(), and fork 259 processes to wrap the shared memory attach count to -32,643.
  • Perform heap grooming and layout, using metrics from sysctl(KERN_MALLOCSTATS) (such as kb_total and kb_totalfree) to track allocations and determine when new pages are allocated.
  • Win the race condition using IPC_RMID in one process while attaching a new size-confused shared memory segment in a helper process.
  • Align IP socket allocations and set IP_MULTICAST_TTL to a non-default value of 2 to allocate a persistent 16-byte struct ip_moptions. Its final word packs two 16-bit counters: imo + 12 = imo_num_memberships | imo_max_memberships << 16.
  • Trigger the conditional -1 out-of-bounds write to overwrite both the number of memberships and maximum memberships fields.
  • close() the socket to traverse the group members, triggering atomic decrements that modify the PTE self-referential mapping twice, switching it from user to supervisor accessible mapping, and achieving kernel code execution by overwriting a predictable kernel pointer.
  • Clean up shared memory accounting and restore the overwritten kernel pointer to obtain a root shell.

That's the short of the matter, the longer version is more interesting, including the history of the vulnerability, as a short shm_nattch can be traced back ~37 years ago, in the original BSD sources.

Taking a step back, this vulnerability ended up getting code execution via a write what where primitive, where the write was caused by a TAILQ_REMOVE, the what was our userland memory mapping that was made supervisor mode accessible to bypass SMAP/SMEP, and the where was a predictable kernel pointer location.

Exploit mitigation

While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization. Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware. When these predictable structure allocations contain function pointers, they become ideal targets for exploitation. For instance, the exploit reliably targets the lo0 and enc0 ioctl handlers, overwriting one to gain control flow and using the other to restore the overwritten pointer.

Aside from the aforementioned errata fixes, there's several other approaches that can be taken to either eliminate or reduce the likelihood of those avenues being used again.

Firstly, we can implement safe-unlinking, a technique that checks doubly linked list invariants before performing the unlink memory writes. If the invariants are violated, then a suitable abort() or panic() is called, depending on if user mode or kernel mode, preventing memory corruption from occurring. An example implementation is here. FreeBSD and NetBSD have an implementation of safe-unlinking in their sys/queue.h implementation.

Secondly, we can randomize the self-referential PTE map allocation address so that the targeted atomic decrement locations would not be possible. This is done by using a random byte (.openbsd.randomdata) and selecting a PML4 slot (320 + (random_byte & 127)) at boot time, and installing the recursive entry at that location. The PTE_BASE definition becomes a runtime expression, yielding bases from 0xffffa00000000000 through 0xffffdf8000000000 at 512-GiB intervals. An example implementation is here. In case randomization is not suitable, other options might suffice, such as marking the PTE as read-only, and changing CR0.WP during modification.

Thirdly, the kernel allocator can be made non-deterministic using two approaches; by randomizing the base address where memory allocations occur at boot time, and additionally randomizing the allocation order at run time. The base address randomization is effectively free as the gap it creates can still be used later on; while runtime randomization does incur some overhead during allocation - it may be possible that more in-depth allocator changes could alleviate this impact. Either approach would be sufficient to break the predictable pointer location without additional vulnerabilities, be it software or hardware.

Furthermore, there are existing and upcoming compiler features that can be used to mitigate against entire vulnerabilities, from array bounds sanitizer (a subset of Undefined Behaviour sanitizer) which can eliminate out of bounds fixed size array accesses. Calif has suggested to FreeBSD that the array bounds sanitizer may make a useful exploit mitigation that can be enabled in release builds, along with privately reporting 21 issues that the array bounds sanitizer would have caught; some with local privilege escalation security impact. An upcoming compiler feature that can be used to help mitigate against heap issues is Alloc Tokens, which can be used to isolate pointer containing allocations from non-pointer allocations. This isolation can make overflows from the non-pointer containing allocation much more difficult to exploit by preventing pointer access, along with making vulnerability classes like Use-after-Free unable to use the opposite type of allocation as the replacement memory allocation.

Since its inception, OpenBSD has consistently championed proactive security through source code auditing, the replacement of insecure APIs, advanced password hashing, cryptography, privilege separation, sandboxing, along with memory safety via ASLR and W^X; frequently setting the standard for system and network hardening.

By proactively hardening, and adapting new and existing mitigation options, we can often systematically neutralize entire classes of exploitation primitives; or at the very least, increase the attacker's cost (i.e. additional time investment, additional vulnerabilities needed to exploit an issue, find alternative avenues, etc). Investing in defensive improvements before vulnerabilities are actively targeted raises the bar for attackers, helping ensure robust protection and long-term resilience. In the age of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, mitigating against entire vulnerability classes, combined with increasing attack complexity only becomes more critical.

item.title: What on Earth Is Dekton? (146 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.worksinprogress.news/p/porcelain, See on Hacker News

This is our fifth article from Issue 26, which arrived with print subscribers last week. In it, Charles C Mann explains how he learned to love porcelain.

I am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife.

My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain.

Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties.

Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history.

The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. Kaolin was known for its color, useful in paints, coatings, and fillers. Potters learned that subjecting this soft, white, unremarkable-looking mud to extreme temperatures produced startling effects.

Ordinary clay looks like amorphous glop but actually is composed of huge numbers of microscopic crystals. The crystals have an unusual structure: flat plates stacked atop each other like playing cards in a deck, loosely held together by hydroxyl groups (hydrogen and oxygen bound together, or -OH, in chemists’ terms). When clay is cooked in a kiln, the hydroxyl groups vibrate and break free, causing the plates to fall apart and reform into long, needle-shaped crystals that lock together into a sturdy structure. Meanwhile, the free hydroxyls merge, becoming water molecules that steam away in the hot kiln, leaving behind oxygen in the new crystals.

Kaolin clay is abundant in kaolinite, a mineral made of aluminum, silicon, oxygen, and hydrogen – Al2Si2O5(OH)4, with the parentheses meaning that each molecule has four hydroxyl groups. When heated in a kiln, kaolinite also loses its hydroxyls and reorganizes itself into a three-dimensional web of needle-like crystals. But when the temperature rises to about 1,200 degrees centigrade, well above the typical level for earthenware pottery, kaolin does something else. The silicon and oxygen break free, forming silica, which forms a thick liquid glass, filling all the spaces around and inside the web of needles, creating a dense, continuous, translucent matrix – porcelain.

In China, like everywhere else, ceramics had been a foundational industry for millennia. Clay was a primary part of construction (bricks, adobe, wattle-and-daub), cooking (pots, tableware), art (paints as well as sculpture), and even communication – clay tablets were the first surfaces used for writing. But porcelain was a giant leap, a concatenation of multiple innovations.

Ordinary kilns couldn’t reach the temperatures required to fire porcelain, partly because their exhaust vents, located on the ‘roof’, let out the hot air almost as fast as it was created, cooling the kiln. (This is a problem for conventional home fireplaces, which are fun to look at in use but wildly inefficient as a means of heating.) Chinese potters designed downdrafts, which forced the hot air to escape through floor vents, trapping the heat around the pottery. Alarmingly, ordinary kilns would shatter or even melt at such high temperatures. Chinese potters invented new types of heat-resistant brick. And so on.

When Europeans first saw East Asian porcelain, probably in the thirteenth century, they were astounded. Harder, stronger, finer, smoother, and more lustrous than any other pottery, it became an obsessive object of desire, ‘white gold’ for the Continent’s wealthy and powerful. Enormous sets of gleaming white china became symbols of luxury – the private jets and invite-only clubs of the Renaissance era.

Unhappy about the high prices charged by the merchants who imported porcelain from Asia, European elites spent lavishly on efforts to make their own porcelain – and failed comprehensively for several centuries.

A key problem was that nobody on the Continent knew that porcelain was made from kaolin. Or that kaolinite alone didn’t actually contain enough glassy liquid silicate to make proper porcelain, so that Chinese potters added pulverized ‘China stone’ – a type of partly decomposed granite containing silicon – into the kaolinite.

Trying to make their wares porcelain-white, European potters added materials like tin oxide and ground glass to the clay, an approach that led to Italian maiolica, French faience, and Delftware. The results were often beautiful, but lacked porcelain’s impermeability to water, high tensile strength, and the distinctive ring made by porcelain cups when tapped with a spoon.

Enter Count Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus (1651–1708), a mathematician, physicist, and philosopher born in the Electorate of Saxony. Tschirnhaus initially studied math and philosophy but in his twenties became fascinated by porcelain. Beginning in about 1679, he conducted a series of experiments that used concave copper mirrors to beam intensely hot sunlight on multiple types of metals, minerals, and ceramics. Eventually he realized that glass lenses could outperform mirrors and invented a method of casting glass to make big, thick lenses for focusing sunlight, sending samples of the results to European monarchs in an unsuccessful quest to obtain financial backing to establish a science academy in Saxony.

In the winter of 1693–94, Tschirnhaus discovered a surprise: a type of clay that wouldn’t melt. Dug from Colditz, about 25 miles southeast of Leipzig, in Saxony, it contained kaolin (Tschirnhaus, of course, didn’t know this). Adding alabaster or chalk to the clay and heating the mix produced a hard, yellow, somewhat translucent ceramic that Tschirnhaus called ‘wax porcelain’. Unfortunately, he couldn’t produce it in quantity – his lenses could focus sunlight on an area of 10 to 15 square centimeters but not heat spaces of any size. When he tried making his porcelain in commercial kilns, their walls shattered or melted. Tschirnhaus was struggling to develop a better kiln when he was approached by Augustus the Strong, the ruler of Saxony.

A few years earlier, a young mountebank in Prussia named Johann Friedrich Böttger had let it be known that he had discovered the Alltinktur, an alchemical substance that cured any disease and turned base metal into gold. In a fine example of FAFO, Prussia’s gold-hungry king, who wanted to monopolize the Alltinktur, immediately ordered Böttger to be taken into ‘protective custody’. Böttger escaped into Saxony, whereupon he was seized by Saxony’s equally gold-hungry ruler Augustus the Strong, confined to an attic in a fortress outside Dresden, and ordered to produce gold. Böttger toiled for years, promising all the while to produce ‘alchymist gold’. Surprisingly, he was unable to deliver. Augustus grew exasperated and in 1704 asked Tschirnhaus to supervise work on the Alltinktur. Tschirnhaus, who evinced no interest in alchemy, invited Böttger to work with him instead on porcelain. To save his neck, Böttger grudgingly agreed.

Tschirnhaus, Böttger, and Gottfried Pabst von Ohain, a high-ranking mining official (in those days, the closest thing available to an earth scientist), developed a red clay that could be made into bricks suitable for porcelain kilns. In June 1708, Pabst von Ohain found a source of white clay – nearly pure kaolin, though he didn’t know it – and shipped it to the other two. Mixing the white clay with ground limestone and heating it in kilns made from the new red clay in August and September, Tschirnhaus single-handedly created a cup that looked and behaved very much like white Chinese porcelain.

He did not live to enjoy his triumph. In October, Tschirnhaus suddenly dropped dead, supposedly of dysentery. On his deathbed, he gave Pabst von Ohain a black box filled with documents. The box was found in Böttger’s belongings after his death, which may explain why he wrote to Augustus in March 1709, claiming to be the sole discoverer of the process to make porcelain. Augustus officially chartered the Royal Porcelain Manufacture in Meissen, another small town near Dresden, the following year and put Böttger in charge. It took ten more years for its workers to figure out that ‘China clay’ (or, more precisely, a similar local stone) was a better additive than limestone. Meissen then became Europe’s porcelain center. Augustus made so much money that he built a ‘Japanese palace’, filled it with Meissen copies of Asian originals, and crowed to visitors that he had beaten the Chinese – correctly, because Meissen porcelain was harder and less porous than the original.

If Meissen was Porcelain 2.0, the Dekton for my cooktop is Porcelain 3.0 or more. Made by baking a slurry of ground porcelain, glass, and quartz into slabs, running the slabs through a huge hydraulic press that applies 25,000 metric tons of pressure, and hardening them at 1,200 degrees centigrade, Dekton took six years and almost $200 million to invent. Traditional ceramics contain microscopic voids and flaws that act as ‘stress concentrators’, focusing rather than diffusing the energy from impacts, which is what causes them to crack. The high pressure and heat used to produce Dekton cause atoms in the particles of kaolinite and quartz to diffuse across the boundaries where they touch, turning the entire thing into what amounts to a single solid mass. In consequence, Dekton has nearly eliminated porcelain’s long-standing weakness: its brittleness and structural fragility.

Dekton is but one part of an ongoing resurgence in porcelain, which itself is part of the still larger revolution in materials science. The field was founded in the 1940s and 1950s, when physicists, chemists, and engineers had to work together in the Second World War, the Cold War, and the space race. But it really took off in the 1980s and 1990s, with the development of precision measuring and manufacturing techniques. Most of its innovations have been incremental, but the accumulated total has had enormous impact in our daily lives.

To give a personal example, my late mother-in-law was injured permanently by slipping on a wet porcelain bathroom tile – something that happens to tens of thousands of people in the United States every year. In the past, firms made nonslip tiles by coating them with rough, jagged grains – a bit like laying sandpaper over the surface, and deservedly unpopular in the home. Ten years ago, Italian and Spanish tile manufacturers like Ceramica Sant’Agostino and Inalco introduced ‘wet-activated’ or ‘in-out’ tiles, with special crystalline compounds baked onto the surface. Dry, they look and feel like ordinary porcelain tiles. But when they are wet and someone steps on them, the pressure drives the water into thousands of pores on the surface, creating a suction-cup effect between foot and tile, instantly making them less slippery. (How much suffering will wet-activated tiles prevent? Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest it would be equivalent, in terms of deaths prevented, to curing childhood cancers.)

Another personal example: My daughter, hit with a rare bone infection at age eleven, now has a porcelain hip joint – porcelain because the previous cobalt and chromium replacement joints can release metal ions into the bloodstream, which can migrate into the placenta of pregnant women, potentially harming the fetus. About the same time that ceramics firms introduced wet-activated tiles, researchers deployed 3D printing to create porous, lattice-like ‘bioceramic’ structures to replace defective bone. The structures are not permanent replacements but scaffolds that allow blood vessels and bone cells to migrate into the spaces in the bioceramic. Over time, the porcelain structure dissolves and is replaced by the patient’s own tissue. (The scaffold is expelled from the body.)

I could go on to talk about the use of nanotechnology to fill porcelain pores to enhance color depth and stain resistance, imprinting porcelain with silver ion layers to enhance antimicrobial activity, or the use of lithium disilicate to make ultrathin dental implants of unprecedented strength. But maybe the best way to say it is that my grandmother, who proudly displayed her mother’s eggshell-thin Meissen china on the sideboard, would have been astonished to find that I was cooking on a thin slab of porcelain, heedlessly dropping heavy pots of boiling water on its surface. But when I tried to explain how remarkable this is to my son, he gave me a blank look. He had never lived in a world that wasn’t made of porcelain.

Charles C Mann is a correspondent for The Atlantic.

URL: https://starskirmish.com/bench/v0-2/, See on Hacker News

TL;DR

  • StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood War
  • Each LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots
  • StarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot

The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness.

An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots.

StarSkirmish Bench v0.2

1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots.

Gemini 4 Argon runs at high, the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at max.

GPT-6 Astra is the top scoring StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 LLM, a clear step ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol in second. Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 are functionally tied behind them, all scoring between 37 and 39.

StarSkirmish Bench vs. Cost

StarSkirmish Bench score against the average API cost of one 1 hour run. Cost is on a log scale.

Muse Wonder Full's pricing is based on Muse Wonder's API pricing.

GPT-6.1 Sol offers uniquely good value: it is the only LLM in the most attractive quadrant, scoring second at just over a tenth of GPT-6 Astra's cost per run.

No Signs of Saturating

The strongest human written bots are still well ahead of every model. Against Stardust, PurpleWave and BananaBrain, the best model, GPT-6 Astra, wins only 7% of its games.

Win rates vs the top human written bots

Average win rate of each model's 5 bots against top human written bots Stardust, PurpleWave, and BananaBrain.

1 hour reasoning limits are a factor, but these matches are played on three 2 player maps. Real human written bot tournament conditions are significantly harder.

New AI Model Highlights

Google and Meta's new flagships replace v0.1's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3: Gemini 4 Argon places 3rd, and Muse Wonder Full 7th. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were covered in v0.1.

AI Model Behaviors

Each run's agent trace records how it spent its hour. The strongest predictor of a model's score is how much it practiced against the 7 strongest bots on the roster.

Win Rates vs. Practice Against Strong Bots

StarSkirmish Bench score against the number of practice games a model's median run played against the 7 strongest roster bots during the hour. The dashed line is a linear fit across the 9 models.

GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon start playing these bots early in the hour, while their own bots still lose to them. Muse Wonder Full, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna rarely or never do. Claude Fable 5.1 is the outlier: it scores 37 while practicing almost entirely against weaker bots.

Run-to-Run Variance

Win rates of each model's 5 runs. Each dot is one run's final bot; the line spans the lowest to the highest run, the bar marks their mean (the model's Bench score) and the band one standard deviation (σ).

Results also vary between runs of the same model. Gemini 4 Argon varies far more than the other labs' flagships: its best and worst runs are 18 points apart, against 9 for GPT-6 Astra and 8 for Claude Opus 5.5.

Implementation Details

Objective

Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against BWAPI 4.4.0, played on OpenBW. Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the BASIL ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins.

The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling.

The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave).

Each model's 5 final bots play each of the 13 roster bots, the 10 competitive human written bots and the 3 demo bots, 6 times on each map, on fresh seeds. Unlike v0.1, the LLM bots don't play each other.

Harness and Reasoning

StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 ran every model in the same harness at 'high' reasoning. v0.2 runs each model in its lab's 1st party CLI harness at the highest reasoning setting it offers.

Harness

Every v0.2 harness compacts the model's context at about 250k tokens. When a conversation nears that point, the CLI condenses it and the model carries on. Codex, OpenAI's CLI, for example, gives the GPT models its default 272k token window and triggers compression once 90% filled.

The CLIs' web search and web fetch tools are turned off, and the agent has no other internet access. The CLI is installed before the clock starts, and the hour counts from when the agent starts. There is no submit tool: the harness collects the bot when the time runs out.

Scoring

v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won).

Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field.

Benchmark Correlations

StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here.

Benchmark Correlation

Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit.

WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing.

StarSkirmish still tracks Vals IOI, olympiad programming problems solved in C++, and WeirdML, an independent benchmark of unusual machine learning coding tasks. One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.

item.title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio (277 pts)
item.description:

content type Featured highlight

MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1), well above average human reading speed.

Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.

We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio, using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post. We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.

We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).

Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark. For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:

mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.

Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively.

Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2, we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.

Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6× faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.

Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6× faster tokens/s.

The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.

While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.

MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch, a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline

In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).

In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.

It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk kk, the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k+1k+1, so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.

Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.

With MLX’s high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1

Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.

With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.

The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s — the two-cable value reported in Table 2, the one-cable run being an additional experiment.

Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with:

mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \
mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080

As with mlx_lm.benchmark, the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode, which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4",
  "provider": {
    "mlx": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Local MLX",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4": {
          "name": "Muse Spark Open 816B (MLX)"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach.

Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.
